segment:
The air was cool. It pressed into her hot lungs and didn’t seem to help. She needed to be cold: cold enough not to feel anything.
His pace was neither fast nor slow. His eyes stayed on the ground as he walked. His feet made little thudding noises on the pavement, rhythmic without trying. Mara didn’t want to walk with him. She wanted to fall down at the base of the steps and cry and then keep sleeping until morning. She needed him to walk with her, or she would stop.
The silence between them was a tangible wall. They reached the end of the driveway. He didn’t say anything at all as he turned right instead of left toward the main highway. No destination seemed in mind—just the opposite direction of where they should have been going.
Mara matched his footsteps automatically, and then they had crossed the street and were walking on the sidewalk under the trees along the road. She took a breath to say something, to offer a comment or question, but he turned his head away and let the silence grow louder. It pressed against her ears, a barrier between them.
His slow breathing sounded steady and sure, as though he could go on like this indefinitely, but he kept it to himself; he didn’t offer her anything but silence and that regular breath.
Mara wondered if he was still in shock. She knew how he must feel: the disorientation after a night of sleep deprivation, the lack of time to sort through emotions. No one would talk about what had happened because it had just happened.
He kept his eyes on the ground and didn’t look up once as they passed other cars on the road. He seemed to be breathing at random, with no sense of sequence or purpose, yet he walked forward, always turning right when he reached a corner. He had a destination; it was not the hotel where she was staying tonight, but neither was it in sight nor did he acknowledge its presence in the world.
The silence was a weight on Mara’s shoulders, heavier than any other she could think of, and Jonah seemed to enjoy it: he was taking his time, breathing easily, as though there were no one else around and nothing to distract him from his own thoughts.
The air grew cooler as they continued on through the empty streets, and Mara was shivering now, unable to stop herself. He had always been a slow talker; he had always been more interested in what she thought than what she felt.
Now he looked at her with something like pity on his face—she knew the emotion but couldn’t remember seeing it on him before—and she wanted to ask him why he was being silent, why he was going so slowly. Why he had said nothing about what had happened tonight.
text:
They started at Fulcrum’s front steps, an instant after the last of the lab staff had gone indoors and locked up. Mara’s mouth felt raw and dry; her throat ached, and her shoulders were rigid and aching too. Her entire body was too hot despite the cold, and she didn’t feel the chill of the night air.
The others were gone. Jonah stood silently beside her, waiting. He was six inches taller than she was. He wasn’t looking at her; his head turned toward the empty drive, and he stared into the darkness beyond the lighted entrance. There was nothing there. She didn’t look. She watched him instead.
“I guess it’s time to go home.” Jonah’s voice was soft, almost inaudible. She had expected more after tonight: analysis or commiseration. Instead he turned sideways with a small sigh and started down the front steps. He swung both arms easily, as though he were on an ordinary walk, though it was the middle of the night and they were both on their way back to hotel rooms in a town she didn’t know.
She followed, trying to match his step. His dark hair rustled as he moved, a low whisper that went with the sound of his breathing: slow, even, no sign of anxiety.

segment:
He took long strides, as if he were out for a morning jog. It was all so easy, he seemed to say, but she couldn’t match his pace and still think about it.
“Jonah,” she said, a little short of breath, “wait a minute.”
He stopped at once, turned back toward her. His stride had been deliberate, not automatic. He hadn’t been hurrying to get away.
The front of his jacket was rumpled. She couldn’t see his face in the darkness. He held the lapels together with both hands, as though he might button it, but there were no buttons. He didn’t seem to be shivering.
She didn’t know where he’d gone in his thoughts, what he’d seen. She only knew she wasn’t with him. He was a shape moving beside her, dark against the cold black sky. She felt cold inside, even though the night was warm enough and she wore a light coat over jeans and a sweatshirt. Her hair smelled of the heavy perfume of a colleague’s expensive body spray; it made her want to throw up. Her hair was still damp with it.
They turned off the main drive, walked north toward town under the moonlight. He kept his hands in his pockets. The night was very quiet.
Mara glanced down, saw the darkness of her own feet as they moved along the drive. They made no noise on the blacktop. Her sneakers were still clean. Her jeans smelled of the artificial flowers in the woman’s bathroom. Jonah smelled like the man he’d been today. He didn’t notice. His steps fell steadily, quietly behind hers. He wasn’t asking her questions.
She walked at him, then past him again. She reached for his arm. His jacket was wet and rough. It was soft underneath. Her palm was cold on his skin; she let go. She’d meant to feel his warmth. She had only imagined it. He smelled of the sweat that ran down her legs when she walked, even in the evening air. She couldn’t see him under his clothes, but she knew what he looked like; she could make him out of her own sweat and hair.
The sidewalk was rough underfoot, cold and damp against her bare feet. They were damp too from the sweat that ran down her legs. His hand touched her lightly on the nape of the neck, where it was bare under her hair. He didn’t touch anywhere else. She wanted to turn around and ask him what he was doing, but she couldn’t move her head. She couldn’t remember what his face looked like, only that he was tall and thin. His hands were long, the nails trimmed short; the fingernails of one hand were stained with ink from signing papers.

segment:
His shirt hung loose over his shoulders, and the thin cotton barely moved as he breathed.
The moon was full, and its light on the pavement had the same blue-white cast as Fulcrum’s bright front lamps. Jonah was bareheaded, and she could see his skin: the hollow in his throat, the straight line of his jaw. He looked younger than thirty—younger even than his real age, like a boy pretending to be a man.
He paused at the bottom step to wait for her. A few paces into the street, he glanced over at her. His eyes were almost black, and he was watching her intently, though his voice was calm as he spoke. “It’s a long walk, Mara.”
Her tongue tasted like cotton. “You can take a cab if you want to, Jonah.” She had said something similar once before, a week ago, when he offered to drive her home. He had declined the offer then. He wouldn’t offer again; that wasn’t his style. If he wanted to ask a ride, he would just ask.
He looked at her for a moment, then turned away. “It’s easier to get back this way.” He took another step and hesitated again. “Do you want a ride?” His voice had an odd note in it, almost like hesitation: the soft sound of someone else’s breath on a microphone. She hadn’t expected that. She wouldn’t know how to answer if she tried, so she just kept following him.
She didn’t know where he was going; they were on a side street now. Her mouth felt thick and heavy when she spoke, her voice low and rough. “I don’t know where I’m going.”
Jonah stopped. The street was almost empty this late. A taxi passed a few blocks away, the lights on its rooftop flashing the yellow reflection of Fulcrum’s entrance on the asphalt. Jonah turned back to look at her, his head slightly tilted. “I can go home with you,” he said.
She had wanted to walk home; she had told him so before he left Fulcrum that evening. She hadn’t meant to change her mind; she couldn’t explain why she had. “No. It’s okay.” She forced herself to stand still, trying not to move at all.
She wasn’t breathing; she couldn’t feel it at all. Her heart pounded in her ears as though it were a clock, ticking out the seconds in an empty room. The cold wind felt like knives slicing through her shirt; she shivered, but there was no relief from it. “It’s just easier to get back this way.” She said that again because he had said it first, and it sounded better than what she wanted to say: It would be better for me not to go home.

segment:
She felt her own breath grow ragged despite herself and pulled in sharply on her diaphragm to bring it under control.
Jonah said nothing more, and Mara was relieved. She couldn’t have talked right now, even if she’d wanted to. She wasn’t ready to face him, or to meet his gaze. The air tasted gritty, like dust after a long rainless season. Her breath came in fast, harsh little rasps as the cold stung her throat.
Jonah moved across the street and turned toward town. He walked at the pace of a person with nowhere special to be, not hurrying or loitering. She felt like a spy as she followed his lead. If he stopped to admire the moon or a flower or a passing dog, would she stop too? Would she stand by his side in silence while he took his time, or would she go home alone? She wanted to know. She wanted him to be the one to decide.
His presence steadied her as they moved slowly along the quiet street. Her ragged breath settled to a quieter rhythm, and the dry dustiness of her throat lessened. Her neck and shoulders began to ease as well.
When Jonah did stop, he stopped short enough to surprise her, and she nearly bumped into him. They were on the sidewalk beside a small house with a bright moonflower vine trailing from the windowsills. The vine was overgrown; it made a pale arch over the steps, and hung down in great dripping lanyards from the eaves.
Jonah stared up at it. His breath stopped so fast that she realized she had been reading his breathing almost since she got outside, checking his pace against her own. She didn’t consciously try to watch, but somehow his movement made a framework for hers. Without it, her breath stopped too, as though they were sharing an invisible thread of air.
She heard herself pull in a quick gasp and felt his head jerk to look at her face. His eyes were open wide; his eyebrows went up and he parted his lips. He hesitated for a second, and then gave a slow, sad laugh that seemed to echo hers. “I’m sorry,” he whispered, as though she had been hurt.
He stepped away from the vine toward her with his hand held out flat, palms down, as though offering a gift she couldn’t see. His eyes were kind and clear in the moonlight. They stayed that way. He didn’t look away or take back his gesture. She could feel the tension between them grow again, but it was different from what they had shared inside. The distance this time seemed real enough to reach out and touch.

segment:
He was moving away from her. If she wanted to keep up, she would have to catch up. She took a deeper breath and did it.
The pavement was cold under her shoes. The air felt cooler than the stones; she could see her breath. It was only a few degrees below freezing.
She had forgotten the wind, had barely noticed it before. She shivered as it caught the front of her coat. It felt like fingers.
They walked in silence down the wide, curving driveway. Fulcrum’s lights were behind them: soft white squares fading as she glanced backward.
The cold air felt good. A slight breeze made the oak branches shift. Leaves rattled and squeaked against one another; she heard small thumps as they dropped to the ground. She saw one of her own steps before she took it. It was dark around her, and she was glad that she couldn’t see Jonah’s face.
Her left ankle protested. She shifted her weight onto her right foot, then back, testing.
She had never hurt an ankle before. The pain wasn’t severe. The ankle didn’t look swollen. If it ached in the morning, she would walk slowly. Or find one of those rented scooters like the one she had seen in San Francisco last year.
Or take a day off, which could mean sleeping until noon. It could mean working in bed on her own research notes. She imagined opening an expensive bottle of wine with dinner, though she wasn’t sure she had anything that would go with pizza.
“We’ll have to walk up Main,” Jonah said. His voice made her start; she nearly bumped into him. He was walking slowly enough to keep pace with her, which meant that he must know how she felt. He hadn’t looked back at her once since they left Fulcrum.
Her head and shoulders ached. Her entire body was too hot; the cold outside seemed good. It made her feel less exposed, as though there were armor between them now.
She had only a short way to walk. She didn’t say this aloud, but she thought it. She wondered what Jonah thought of her silence, of her failure to initiate conversation, even when it was necessary to say that he was right. The route he had chosen would not take her home, but she didn’t say this either.
She couldn’t think of anything to say. She hadn’t planned tonight’s session; she was barely speaking now because she couldn’t get a new word order out. She wondered whether she sounded as flat and dull as she felt. She wondered what Jonah wanted her to say. If she were able to read him like an experimenter, she might have some idea. If he had been willing to play a game.
